import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 109

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/109](https://www.erdosproblems.com/109)
- [MRR19] J. Moreira, F.K. Richter, and D. Robertson, A proof of a sumset conjecture of Erdős,
  Annals of Math. 189 (2019), 605-652.
-/

open Pointwise

namespace Erdos109

/--
Any $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of positive upper density contains a sumset $B+C$ where both $B$ and $C$
are infinite.

The Erdős sumset conjecture. Proved by Moreira, Richter, and Robertson [MRR19].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem erdos_109 (A : Set ℕ) (h : A.upperDensity > 0) :
    ∃ B C : Set ℕ, B.Infinite ∧ C.Infinite ∧ B + C ⊆ A := by
  sorry

end Erdos109

reformulations.difference: The imported upperDensity counts A ∩ {0,…,n−1}, whereas MRR19 Conjecture 1.1 counts A ∩ {1,…,n}. Lean also permits zero in the summand sets.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For n ≥ 1, the two counts differ by 1_{0∈A} − 1_{n∈A}, so their normalized ratios differ by at most 1/n and have identical limsups. The value at n = 0 does not affect the limsup. If the source's natural numbers are interpreted as positive integers, deleting zero from A preserves density, and deleting zero from each infinite summand preserves infinitude and shrinks the sumset. Thus that convention also leaves the problem unchanged. The witness-removal equivalence was proved in the scratch file; the density-endpoint equivalence was checked mathematically, not proved in Lean.

sources_consulted: Moreira, Richter, and Robertson, A proof of a sumset conjecture of Erdős, arXiv:1803.00498v6: Conjecture 1.1, Theorem 1.2, and concluding questions. LaTeX source: https://arxiv.org/e-print/1803.00498v6
review.notes: The sole declaration faithfully states the original Erdős sumset conjecture. The source records an affirmative solution, now also Lean-verified, consistent with research solved. Checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiled successfully: the density uses real division and defaults to the ambient set univ; finite sets have upper density 0, univ has density 1, and even numbers have density 1/2; pointwise addition requires every cross-sum. All cardinalities in the density formula count finite intersections, and division by zero at the initial index is harmless. The reviewed file was not modified.
